design-controls-s1.title: The grease-spot test
design-controls-s1.html:
Fats and oils (lipids) are hydrophobic: they soak into paper and do not evaporate, leaving a see-through (translucent) spot. Water also makes paper see-through, but only until it evaporates. A class rubbed each sample onto brown paper, waited 30 minutes, then held the paper up to a light.

Grease-spot results after 30 minutes of drying

Distilled waterNo

design-null-hypothesis-s2.title: Does cholesterol change membrane fluidity?
design-null-hypothesis-s2.html:
A team made artificial membranes from the same phospholipids, with and without added cholesterol. At 10 °C they measured how fast a labeled lipid moved sideways within the membrane: faster sideways movement means a more fluid membrane. Six membranes of each type were tested.

Results: without cholesterol, mean 2.1 µm²/s (individual values 1.9 to 2.3); with cholesterol, mean 2.9 µm²/s (individual values 2.7 to 3.1).

design-prediction-mechanism-s1.title: A poison and the electron transport chain
design-prediction-mechanism-s1.html:
In the inner mitochondrial membrane, NADH and FADH₂ hand electrons to a chain of proteins. As electrons pass along, the proteins pump H⁺ into the intermembrane space; at the end, electrons combine with O₂ and H⁺ to form water. H⁺ flowing back through ATP synthase drives ATP production.

Cyanide binds the last protein of the chain and stops it from passing electrons to O₂. A researcher treats cultured muscle cells, which can also carry out lactic acid fermentation, with a low dose of cyanide.

design-prediction-mechanism-s2.html:

items.q: In this investigation, what are the independent and dependent variables?
options: Independent: width of the strip. Dependent: height the water climbed in 10 minutes.
Independent: height the water climbed. Dependent: width of the strip the student cut.
Independent: the type of filter paper. Dependent: the time the strips were left in water.
Independent: the 10-minute time limit. Dependent: the width and the height of each wet strip.

items.q: Select ALL of the factors that were controlled variables in this investigation.
options: Type of paper
Width of the strip
Time before measuring
Height of the wet front
Mean height for each width

items.q: Which conclusion do these data support?
options: Over this range, strip width had no clear effect on how high water climbed in 10 minutes.
Wider strips pulled water higher, because a wider strip has more paper for water to stick to.
Narrower strips pulled water higher, because their mean height at 0.5 cm was the largest value.
The investigation failed, because a well-designed experiment shows a difference between groups.

items.q: Water climbs paper because water molecules are attracted to the paper fibers (adhesion) and to each other (cohesion). Which testable question would best follow from these results?
options: Does the type of paper affect how high water climbs in 10 minutes?
Why does water like to climb up paper instead of staying in the beaker?
Is filter paper the most interesting paper for studying water?
Would water climb a strip faster if the strip wanted to get wet?

items.q: Which feature of the procedure most weakens the conclusion that temperature alone caused the 40 °C dishes to lose the most water?
options: Only the 40 °C cabinet had a fan, so moving air was a second difference between the groups.
Three dishes per temperature is too few repeats for any comparison of the means to be made.
The dishes were weighed at the start, which could have disturbed the water before the experiment.
Mass of water lost is a dependent variable, so it is not possible to control it during the experiment.

items.q: What percentage of its starting 50.0 g of water did a typical 30 °C dish lose in 24 hours (use the mean)? Give your answer to the nearest whole percent.
Which is the best if-then prediction for this experiment?
options: If the water temperature is higher, then more water will evaporate in 24 hours, because more molecules have enough energy to break their hydrogen bonds and escape.
If water evaporates, then the temperature of the cabinet will rise, because evaporation releases heat into the surrounding air and warms the inside of each cabinet.
If the dishes are identical, then the experiment will be fair, because identical dishes hold the same mass of water.
If more water is lost, then the temperature was higher, because hot water evaporates.

items.q: The class wants a group that shows how much water an open dish loses with no warming at all. Which addition is the best control group?
options: Three identical dishes of 50.0 g water left at room temperature in a cabinet that is switched off, with no fan
Three dishes of 50.0 g water at 50 °C, to extend the range of temperatures that were tested
One dish of 50.0 g water sealed with a lid in the 40 °C cabinet, to show what happens when no water can escape the dish
Three dishes holding 100.0 g of water at 20 °C, so that more water is available to evaporate

items.q: A student puts ice cubes of equal mass into cups of water at 10, 25 and 40 °C and times how long each cube takes to melt. Which variable is the dependent variable?
options: Time for the ice cube to melt
Starting temperature of the water
Mass of each ice cube
Volume of water in each cup

items.q: To test whether salt affects how fast water cools, a student puts plain water in a glass beaker and salt water in a plastic cup, heats both and times the cooling. What is the main problem with this design?
options: The container differs as well as the salt, so a difference in cooling time could come from either one.
The student should measure temperature instead of time, because time is not a dependent variable.
Salt water and plain water are different liquids, so comparing the two in one experiment is not a fair test.
There is no hypothesis, and an experiment run without a written hypothesis produces no usable data.

items.q: Which question is testable in a controlled experiment?
options: Does adding soap change the number of drops of water a coin can hold?
Is water the most important substance for living things on Earth?
Why do water molecules prefer to stay close to each other?
Should students drink more water during exams to stay alert?

items.q: Why does a well-designed experiment test each condition several times?
options: Repeats show how much the results vary by chance, so a real difference between groups can be told apart from that variation.
Repeats make each individual measurement more accurate, because the equipment warms up and settles after the first use in a session.
Repeats guarantee that the hypothesis is correct, as long as the repeats give matching results.
Repeats let the investigator choose the result that best fits the prediction and report that one.

items.q: What is the difference between a control group and a controlled variable?
options: A control group is a whole group given the baseline condition; a controlled variable is one factor kept the same in every group.
A control group is the group kept at room temperature; a controlled variable is the factor the investigator deliberately changes between groups.
They are two names for the same thing: anything in the experiment that the investigator does not change.
A controlled variable is the group with no treatment; a control group is the factor kept the same everywhere.

items.q: Put the steps of planning a controlled experiment on evaporation in a sensible order.
options: Write a testable question: does temperature affect evaporation?
Choose the independent variable and its values (20, 30 and 40 °C).
Decide how to measure the response at each of those temperatures (mass lost in 24 h).
List the controlled variables (dish, starting mass, air movement, time).
Run several dishes at each temperature and record every value.

items.q: A student predicts: "If the water is warmer, then it will climb filter paper faster, because warm water molecules move faster." She finds warm and cold water climb to the same height in 10 minutes. What do these results show about the prediction?
options: The results do not support the prediction about height at 10 minutes, but speed early in the climb might still differ.
The prediction is proven wrong, so faster-moving molecules can have no effect on how water travels through paper of any kind.
The results support the prediction, because both samples of water climbed the paper strip.
The results tell her nothing, because the student did not use a control group with no water.

items.q: Which sample is the negative control, and what possibility does it rule out?
options: Distilled water; it rules out that the paper or the procedure makes a lasting spot without any fat.
Vegetable oil; it rules out that the test fails to detect fat on this paper on this day.
Apple slice; it rules out that foods from plants contain fat, since apples come from plants.
Distilled water; it rules out that the foods were contaminated with extra water before the test began on the paper.

items.q: Suppose the vegetable oil had left no spot. What could the class conclude about the apple's "No" result?
options: Nothing reliable: the test failed to detect a known fat, so the apple could contain fat that was missed.
The apple contains no fat, because its result matches the result for the vegetable oil.
The apple contains more fat than the oil, because neither of them left a spot on the paper.
The apple contains no fat, because the water also left no spot, which shows that the negative control worked properly.

items.q: A student checks the paper after 2 minutes instead of 30 and records "Yes" for the apple slice. What most likely explains this result?
options: The apple's juice, which is mostly water, had not yet evaporated, so wetness made a spot that would have faded.
The apple contains a large amount of fat, which slowly evaporates from the paper over the 30 minutes.
Water is hydrophobic, so the apple's water soaked into the paper and stayed there like an oil would.
Checking early made the test more sensitive, so the "Yes" at 2 minutes is the correct reading for the apple.

items.q: Which claim about the unknown powder is best supported, given both controls behaved as expected?
options: The powder probably contains some fat, but less than the peanut, because its spot was faint rather than large.
The powder contains no fat, because a faint spot is closer to the water result than it is to the large spot made by the oil.
The powder is pure fat, because a lasting spot means the sample is made of lipid alone.
Nothing can be said, because the powder was not tested alongside a positive control.

items.q: Which result shows that the experiment has a problem?
options: Tube 2, because distilled water should stay orange-brown with iodine.
Tube 1, because starch solution should stay orange-brown with iodine.
Tube 3, because potato extract is expected to be free of starch.
Tube 5, because vegetable oil should turn fully blue-black.

items.q: What is the most likely cause of the blue-black color in the tubes of distilled water and sugar water?
options: Starch carried over in the shared wash water coated every tube, contaminating them before the samples went in.
Table sugar is a polysaccharide made of glucose, so it reacts with iodine just as starch does.
Iodine turns blue-black on its own after several minutes in a tube, whether or not starch is present in the solution.
Distilled water breaks down into starch when iodine is added, by dehydration synthesis of water molecules.

items.q: What should the student do next?
options: Repeat the whole test with new, separately rinsed tubes, including both controls.
Keep the results for tubes 3 and 5, since those are the foods of real interest here.
Drop tube 2 from the report, since a control is not part of the actual results.
Report that sugar contains starch, since tube 4 turned the same color as tube 1.

items.q: In this experiment, what role does tube 1 (starch solution) play?
options: Positive control: it shows the iodine can detect starch.
Negative control: it shows what a starch-free tube looks like.
Independent variable: it is the factor the student changed.
Test sample: it is one of the foods being identified.

items.q: A student tests whether saturated fats melt at higher temperatures than unsaturated fats. She buys butter from one store and olive oil from another, and heats each in a different pan on a different stove. Which factor is most likely to be confounding?
options: The pans and stoves heat at different speeds, which could change the measured melting point.
The type of fat, because saturated and unsaturated fats differ in their structure.
The temperature at which each fat melts, which the student reads off a thermometer.
The stores where the fats were bought, because one of them sells more expensive brands.

items.q: A test for fat uses a red dye that dissolves into lipids and colors them. Select ALL samples that would make a good positive control.
options: Vegetable oil
Distilled water
The red dye dissolved in water
Table sugar dissolved in water
The unknown food being tested

items.q: An exam answer says: "The control is the tube of water, because it is the control." Which addition would best earn the point for justifying the control?
options: "…because water contains no starch, so if it stays orange-brown, color changes in the food tubes are not caused by the tubes or the iodine."
"…because water is the standard control in most biology experiments, so the teacher will expect to see a water tube listed in the data table."
"…because water is a clear liquid, so it is easy to see whether the color of the iodine changes."
"…because the control has to be kept the same as the other tubes, so it should contain nothing of its own."

items.q: To test whether a new paper detects fat more reliably than ordinary brown paper, a student uses peanut on both papers. What is the best negative control?
options: Distilled water rubbed onto both kinds of paper in the same way
Vegetable oil rubbed onto both kinds of paper in the same way
Peanut rubbed onto the new paper and read after 2 minutes
A blank sheet of each paper that is left untouched on the bench

items.q: What does a positive control rule out?
options: That a negative result happened because the test was not working
That a positive result happened because of contamination
That the independent variable was changed between groups
That repeated trials gave different results by chance

items.q: Two groups compared how much fat is in two brands of chips by weighing the grease spot each made. Group 1 used 5.0 g of brand X; group 2 used 2.0 g of brand Y and read the paper an hour later. Select ALL factors that are confounding.
options: Mass of chips used
Time before the paper was read
Brand of chips
Mass of the grease spot
Type of brown paper used by both groups

items.q: In a new run of the grease-spot test, the water leaves a lasting see-through spot and so does every food. Which explanation, if true, would account for both results?
options: Students rubbed on every sample with fingers still greasy from the oil, so each spot got some lipid.
The foods contained more fat than usual, because they were bought from a different store this time.
The paper was too thin, so it could not show spots from any sample, including the oil.
Water is a lipid in small amounts, which is why water spots can last on brown paper.

items.q: Which is the null hypothesis for this experiment?
options: The heating temperature has no effect on how much red color leaks from beet cubes.
Heating beet cubes to higher temperatures increases how much red color leaks out.
Beet cubes heated to 80 °C will turn the water redder than cubes heated to 20 °C.
Heat damages the membranes of beet cells, which lets the red substance escape into the water.

items.q: Compare the 20 °C and 40 °C groups. What is the best decision about the null hypothesis for these two groups?
options: Fail to reject it: the means differ by 0.01, much less than the spread among cubes in either group.
Reject it: the 40 °C mean is higher than the 20 °C mean, so heating to 40 °C increased the leakage.
Accept it: the data prove that heating from 20 °C to 40 °C has no effect on the beet membranes.
Reject it: the four 40 °C values include the highest single reading of the two groups, 0.12.

items.q: Compare the 20 °C and 80 °C groups. What is the best decision?
options: Reject the null hypothesis: every 80 °C value is far above every 20 °C value, too large a gap to blame on chance.
Fail to reject the null hypothesis: four cubes per group is too few to reach a decision about any difference in leakage.
Reject the alternative hypothesis: the 80 °C results are more spread out, so they are less reliable.
Prove the alternative hypothesis: the difference shows that heat causes leakage in beets of any variety or age.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the leakage above 40 °C?
options: Heat disrupts the membrane: the bilayer becomes more fluid and membrane proteins unfold, opening gaps the red substance escapes through.
Heat makes the red substance evaporate from the cells, and it then dissolves back into the water around the cubes.
Heat makes the cell walls of the beet shrink, which squeezes the red substance out through the intact membranes.
Heat causes the beet cells to make more of the red substance, so the same undamaged membranes release a larger amount of it into the water.

items.q: Which is a directional alternative hypothesis for this experiment?
options: Higher heating temperatures increase the amount of red color that leaks from beet cubes.
Heating temperature changes the amount of red color that leaks from beet cubes.
Heating temperature has no effect on the amount of red color leaking from beet cubes.
The amount of red color that leaks from beet cubes depends on the size of the cubes used.

items.q: Which pair correctly states the null and alternative hypotheses for this experiment?
options: H₀: adding cholesterol has no effect on membrane fluidity at 10 °C. H₁: adding cholesterol changes membrane fluidity at 10 °C.
H₀: adding cholesterol makes membranes less fluid at 10 °C. H₁: adding cholesterol makes membranes more fluid at 10 °C.
H₀: cholesterol changes membrane fluidity at 10 °C. H₁: cholesterol has no effect on membrane fluidity at 10 °C.
H₀: membranes are fluid at 10 °C. H₁: membranes are solid at 10 °C whether or not they contain cholesterol.

items.q: What decision do the results support?
options: Reject the null hypothesis: the two groups do not overlap, and the difference in means is large compared with the spread.
Fail to reject the null hypothesis: cholesterol is known to stiffen membranes, so this result is a mistake.
Accept the null hypothesis: both groups of membranes were fluid, so cholesterol made no difference.
Fail to reject the null hypothesis: six membranes per group are too few to support any decision about the effect of cholesterol.

items.q: Which explanation fits the result that cholesterol increased fluidity at 10 °C?
options: Cholesterol wedges between phospholipids and stops their tails from packing tightly together when the membrane is cold.
Cholesterol breaks the covalent bonds inside the phospholipid tails, making each tail shorter and more mobile.
Cholesterol adds double bonds to the phospholipid tails, turning saturated tails into unsaturated tails.
Cholesterol is a protein that pushes lipids sideways through the membrane, so the labeled lipid moved faster.

items.q: For the comparison to test the null hypothesis fairly, which factors had to be the same for both kinds of membrane?
options: The kind of phospholipid and the temperature
The amount of cholesterol in each membrane
The speed at which the labeled lipid moved sideways
The number of membranes, which could differ freely between the groups

items.q: An experiment fails to reject the null hypothesis. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The data did not show an effect of the independent variable; an effect could still exist that this experiment was unable to detect.
The null hypothesis has been proved true, so the independent variable has no effect under any conditions.
The experiment was a failure, because a well-designed experiment rejects the null hypothesis it was built to test, or it was not run properly.
The alternative hypothesis has been proved true, because the null hypothesis could not be rejected.

items.q: A student tests whether the amount of salt in water affects how far a beet cube's color spreads into it. Which is a correct null hypothesis?
options: Salt concentration has no effect on how far the color spreads.
More salt will make the color spread farther into the water.
If salt is added, then the color will spread less into the water.
Salt water and plain water will give different amounts of spreading.

items.q: Which statement uses the language of hypothesis testing correctly?
options: "The difference between groups was large compared with the variation within them, so we reject the null hypothesis."
"The results prove our hypothesis that heat damages beet membranes, so we accept the alternative hypothesis."
"There was no difference between the groups, so we accept the null hypothesis and conclude heat has no effect."
"The 80 °C cubes leaked more, so we reject the alternative hypothesis and accept the null hypothesis."

items.q: Select ALL statements that are null hypotheses.
options: There is no difference in membrane fluidity between membranes with and without cholesterol.
Membranes with cholesterol will be more fluid at 10 °C.
The temperature at which beet cubes are heated is not related to the amount of color that leaks.
Beet cubes from older beets will leak more color than those from younger beets.
Membranes with cholesterol are better for cells.

items.q: Why does an investigation test the null hypothesis rather than trying to prove the alternative directly?
options: A "no effect" statement predicts what the data should look like, so data far from that pattern can count against it.
The null hypothesis is the one the investigator believes, so it is fairer to test it first and then the other.
The alternative hypothesis can be tested just once the null hypothesis has been accepted by an earlier study.
Testing the null hypothesis requires fewer repeats than testing the alternative, so it saves time and materials in most experiments.

items.q: Put the steps of hypothesis testing in order.
options: State the null and alternative hypotheses.
Design the experiment and collect data from repeated trials.
Compare the difference between groups with the variation within groups.
Decide to reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis.
State whether the data support the alternative hypothesis.

items.q: Two groups of 3 membranes each give fluidity values of 2.0, 2.6, 3.2 and 2.4, 3.0, 3.6 µm²/s. The second group's mean is 0.4 higher. Which is the best conclusion?
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis, because the groups overlap widely and chance could explain the difference.
Reject the null hypothesis, because the second group's mean is higher than the first group's mean.
Reject the null hypothesis, because the highest value of the second group is higher than the first group's.
Accept the null hypothesis, because both groups contain three membranes that were tested in the same way.

items.q: Which is the best claim based on these data?
options: Potato catalase works fastest near pH 7, and its activity falls as the pH moves away in either direction.
Potato catalase works best in acidic conditions, because pH 3 and pH 5 are both below neutral.
Potato catalase is destroyed at each pH other than pH 7, because the rates measured at the other four pH values are lower.
Potato catalase activity rises steadily with pH, because pH 11 is higher than pH 3.

items.q: Which sentence is the best evidence for the claim that catalase works fastest near pH 7?
options: The mean rate at pH 7 (4.8 mL/min) is higher than at pH 5 (2.1) and pH 9 (3.0), and its error bar overlaps neither of theirs.
Catalase is an enzyme, and enzymes have an optimal pH at which their active sites have the right shape.
The graph shows that pH affects catalase, because the bars are different heights at different pH values.
The students did five trials at each pH, so their results are reliable, and a claim based on five trials per group is certainly right.

items.q: Which is the best reasoning to complete the argument?
options: pH changes the charges on R groups in the active site; away from pH 7 this alters the site's shape and how well it binds substrate.
The rate at pH 7 is 4.8 mL/min, which is more than twice the rate at pH 5 and about 1.6 times the rate measured at pH 9, as the graph shows.
Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy, so a faster rate means more oxygen gas is released per minute.
Catalase prefers a neutral environment because the potato cells it comes from need to stay healthy and grow.

items.q: Which is the most important limitation on the claim "catalase works fastest at pH 7"?
options: Only five pH values were tested, two units apart, so the true optimum could be anywhere between about pH 6 and pH 8.
The students used potato extract, which is a natural material and so gives results that are less scientific.
Error bars were drawn on the graph, which shows that the measurements contained mistakes.
Oxygen was measured instead of water, even though both are products of the same reaction.

items.q: Which claim do the data best support?
options: Compound X acts as a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme.
Compound X acts as a noncompetitive inhibitor of the enzyme.
Compound X denatures the enzyme, so it can no longer bind substrate.
Compound X increases the enzyme's maximum rate at high substrate levels.

items.q: Which evidence best supports the claim that compound X competes with the substrate?
options: At 1 mM substrate X cuts the rate by about 58% (3.3 to 1.4), but at 40 mM by only about 8% (9.5 to 8.7).
With compound X, the rate at 40 mM substrate (8.7 µmol/min) is lower than the rate without it (9.5 µmol/min).
Both curves start at zero and rise as the substrate concentration increases from 0 to 40 mM in each tube.
Compound X lowers the rate of the reaction at each of the six substrate concentrations that were tested.

items.q: Which reasoning best links the evidence to the claim?
options: X binds the active site reversibly; as substrate rises, substrate molecules occupy most active sites first, so X's effect shrinks.
X binds the enzyme away from its active site and changes the enzyme's shape, so fewer enzymes work at any substrate level.
X raises the activation energy of the reaction, so more substrate is needed to supply the extra energy that X takes away.
X is a substrate of the enzyme as well, so the enzyme makes product from both of them and the total rate stays the same.

items.q: Which addition would most strengthen the claim that X is competitive rather than noncompetitive?
options: Measuring rates at still higher substrate (80 and 160 mM) to see if the X curve reaches the same maximum.
Repeating the experiment at 10 °C, so that the reaction runs more slowly and is easier to time precisely.
Measuring the rate with compound X alone and no substrate, to see whether X itself is changed by the enzyme.
Testing a second enzyme from a different organism, to see whether X inhibits enzymes from other species.

items.q: A student writes: "(1) Heating amylase above 60 °C stops it from working. (2) At 70 °C the rate was 0.1 mg/min, compared with 4.2 mg/min at 40 °C. (3) High temperature breaks the hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer fits starch. (4) Our water bath may have been warmer than its setting." Select ALL sentences that are reasoning.
options: Sentence 1
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4

items.q: Which is the weakness in this reasoning? "The enzyme works best at 37 °C because the rate was highest at 37 °C."
options: It restates the evidence instead of explaining it with a biological mechanism.
It uses a number, and reasoning should be written without any numbers.
It is too long, because reasoning should be a single word such as "denaturation".
It mentions temperature, which belongs in the evidence part of the answer instead.

items.q: Enzyme activity rises from 10 °C to 40 °C and then falls sharply above 45 °C. Which reasoning explains both parts?
options: Warmer molecules collide more often, raising the rate, until heat breaks the weak bonds holding the active site's shape and the enzyme denatures.
The enzyme makes more copies of itself as the temperature rises, until above 45 °C it runs out of the amino acids it needs to make more copies.
Heat adds activation energy to the substrate, until above 45 °C the substrate has more energy than the active site can hold, so it stops binding.
The substrate dissolves better as the water warms, until above 45 °C it evaporates from the solution and no longer reaches the enzyme.

items.q: In a catalase experiment, students timed how long a paper disk soaked in extract took to float up through hydrogen peroxide. Which is a source of error rather than a design limitation?
options: Different students started and stopped the timer at slightly different moments.
A single kind of potato was used, so the result may not apply to other species.
The pH values tested were spaced two units apart, so the optimum is uncertain.
Temperature was held at 25 °C, so the effect of temperature was not studied.

items.q: What makes evidence strong in a claim-evidence-reasoning answer?
options: It quotes specific values with units and makes the comparison the claim depends on.
It repeats the claim in different words, so the grader sees it is consistent.
It names the biological principle, such as denaturation, without any numbers.
It describes the procedure in detail, so the grader trusts the data.

items.q: Put the parts of a scientific argument in order.
options: Claim: one sentence that answers the question.
Evidence: specific data, with units, that support the claim.
Reasoning: the biological mechanism that explains why the evidence supports the claim.
Limitation: what the data cannot show, and how to address it.

items.q: An enzyme's rate at 30 °C is 5.1 ± 0.6 and at 35 °C is 5.4 ± 0.7 µmol/min (95% CI). Which claim is justified?
options: The data do not show a difference in activity between 30 °C and 35 °C.
The enzyme works faster at 35 °C than at 30 °C, because 5.4 is greater than 5.1.
The enzyme's optimum is 35 °C, because that is the higher of the two rates measured.
Temperature has no effect on this enzyme, because the two rates are about the same.

items.q: Predict how each variable changes in the cyanide-treated muscle cells within a few minutes, compared with untreated cells.

variables.name: O₂ used by the cells per minute
H⁺ gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane

items.q: Which is the best prediction with mechanism for the Krebs cycle in the cyanide-treated cells?
options: It slows, because NADH cannot pass its electrons to the blocked chain, so NAD⁺ runs short and the cycle's oxidation steps cannot continue.
It speeds up, because the cells need more ATP, so they send more pyruvate into the mitochondria to make up the lost ATP.
It stays the same, because the Krebs cycle does not use oxygen directly, so a block at the end of the chain has no route to reach it in the mitochondrion.
It stops at once, because cyanide binds the enzymes of the Krebs cycle as well as the last protein of the chain.

items.q: A student predicts, "The cells will die because they cannot get oxygen." What is the main weakness of this prediction?
options: Oxygen still reaches the cells; the problem is that electrons cannot be passed to it, and no steps link the block to the outcome.
It is too detailed, because a prediction should name just the variable that changes and leave out the cause and any other explanation.
It is wrong, because muscle cells use fermentation for their ATP and are not affected by cyanide in any way.
It uses the word "because", which belongs in reasoning rather than in a prediction about an experiment.

items.q: Which next experiment would best test that cyanide lowers ATP by acting on the electron transport chain rather than on glycolysis?
options: Supply isolated mitochondria with pyruvate and measure their O₂ use with and without cyanide.
Treat the cells with twice the dose of cyanide and measure how much faster they die.
Measure the glucose taken up by cells with and without cyanide over 24 hours.
Grow the cells without glucose so that glycolysis is prevented, and add no cyanide.

items.q: Predict how each variable changes in the DCMU-treated disks after 10 minutes, compared with the control.

variables.name: CO₂ fixed by the Calvin cycle

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the DCMU curve after 5 minutes?
options: With electrons unable to leave photosystem II, it cannot replace them from water, so water splitting and O₂ release stop.
DCMU destroys the chlorophyll in the disks, so they can no longer absorb any of the light energy that reaches them from the lamp.
DCMU blocks the Calvin cycle directly, so O₂ is used up as fast as it is made.
DCMU closes the leaf's stomata, so the O₂ that is made is trapped inside the leaf disk.

items.q: Calculate the control disks' rate of O₂ release between 5 and 15 minutes, in µmol per disk per minute, to two decimal places.
An artificial compound can take electrons directly from photosystem II, before the DCMU block. If it is added to DCMU-treated disks, what is the best prediction?
options: O₂ release resumes, because photosystem II can again pass on electrons and refill them by splitting water.
O₂ release stays at zero, because DCMU still blocks the chain and so no electrons can leave photosystem II.
NADPH production resumes, because the compound carries the electrons on to photosystem I and NADP⁺.
O₂ release rises above the control, because the compound adds extra electrons to photosystem II.

items.q: Which next experiment best tests whether DCMU's effect depends on light?
options: Repeat with DCMU-treated and control disks in the dark, measuring O₂ use, which reflects cellular respiration.
Repeat in brighter light with a stronger lamp, to see whether DCMU can be overcome by more light.
Repeat with more disks per dish, to make the error bars on the O₂ measurements narrower.
Repeat with DCMU added at 10 minutes instead of 5, to see whether timing changes the curve.

items.q: An uncoupler lets H⁺ leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane without passing through ATP synthase. Predict the change in each variable.

variables.name: O₂ used by the electron transport chain

items.q: A competitive inhibitor of an enzyme is added, and then substrate concentration is raised far above normal. Which prediction with mechanism is best?
options: The rate recovers toward normal, because substrate molecules occupy most active sites first, outcompeting the inhibitor.
The rate stays low, because the inhibitor binds elsewhere on the enzyme and changes the active site's shape permanently.
The rate falls to zero, because extra substrate crowds the active site so that neither molecule can bind.
The rate rises above normal, because the inhibitor is converted into extra substrate once substrate is high.

items.q: A drug blocks aquaporins in kidney tubule cells. Which is the best prediction with mechanism?
options: Less water is reabsorbed, because without its channels water crosses the tubule cells' membranes slowly, so the urine is more dilute.
More water is reabsorbed, because blocking aquaporins traps water inside the cells and pulls more in from the tubule.
No change, because water crosses membranes by osmosis, a process that does not involve membrane proteins of any kind in kidney tubule cells.
Less salt is reabsorbed, because aquaporins are the channels that carry sodium ions across the tubule cell membrane.

items.q: Put the steps of a prediction with mechanism in order, for cyanide added to cells.
options: Name the part of the system that is disrupted: the last protein of the electron transport chain.
State what that part can no longer do: pass electrons to O₂.
Trace the next consequence: proton pumping stops and the H⁺ gradient runs down.
State the effect on a measurable variable: ATP production by ATP synthase falls.

items.q: Which statement is a prediction with mechanism rather than a prediction alone?
options: "If a cell is given an uncoupler, its ATP production will fall, because H⁺ leaks back without passing through ATP synthase."
"If a cell is given an uncoupler, its ATP production will fall, and the cell will also release more heat than before."
"Uncouplers are dangerous because they lower ATP and raise body temperature."
"ATP production depends on many factors inside the mitochondrion, and an uncoupler is one of the factors that can change it."

items.q: Cells given a drug use less O₂. A student concludes the drug blocks the electron transport chain. Which next experiment would best rule out the alternative that the drug simply slows glycolysis?
options: Give the drug to isolated mitochondria supplied directly with pyruvate and measure their O₂ use.
Give the drug at three doses to whole cells and measure O₂ use, to show that the effect depends on dose.
Measure O₂ use in whole cells at 25 °C and 37 °C, with the drug added at the same dose each time.
Measure how much glucose the treated cells take up, to see whether it is lower than in untreated cells.
